476.t: Joe's family, the band at his house, and Warren as inspiration
476.s: His parents played guitar and piano; bands gathered at his house until train time, and watching Warren and Edgar made him want to play piano.
476.q: In other words, when they knock off of the job, they come into your house and play until train time.

476.t: Playing with the Watson band in East Christian
476.s: Joe joined the Watson brothers' band, replacing his sister Anita Jackson on piano, after the youth band broke up.
476.q: In New Orleans, I'll tell you what to say after we finish. Uh-oh.

526.t: How her father taught her to write notes, and playing for funerals
526.s: Her father told her to just put dots on paper, which shaped her simple style; she played organ at funerals at eight and led the altos.
526.q: Oh yeah. My father, I remember how all that started. He was giving me a piano lesson and I said, “well now, this music that you’re teaching me now, how did that come into being?” And he said, “well, a composer wrote it.” And I said “well, how did the composer do that?” So he gave me a piece of…

526.t: Pianos tuned a half step low
526.s: Her father tuned the studio pianos a half step low to save money, which she still adjusts for.
526.ch: Marriages, Tong Funeral and Liberation Music
526.q: Well my father was a piano teacher and he taught in the house as well as he would go to people’s houses, you know if they couldn’t come to our house. And he would sit at one piano and the student would sit at the other piano. But the bad thing about this was he had the pianos tuned a half a step…

377.t: The upright piano in the parlor and his mother's aims
377.s: Basie describes the big upright piano at home and says his mother simply wanted him to learn to play, not to become a musician.
377.q: Well, they fit everywhere, you know, like the little Spinets, little pianos like that. There's hardly a place for a big upright piano to go (inaudible).

377.t: His brother, and piano lessons as a neighborhood custom
377.s: Basie had an older brother he barely knew; his mother had a class of children, and the kids went to Mowchow or Holloway.
377.q: Well, I had one brother. I did have one brother, but I knew very little about him. I mean, tell you, they lost him when I was just barely could remember.

66.t: Her mother Virginia Burley and the first melodies on her lap
66.s: Her mother played church piano and organ; Mary Lou picked out melodies at 2 or 3 and her mother called the neighbours. Professional pianists like Jack Howard were brought in to play around her.
66.q: : Virginia Burley, B-u-r-l-e-y. She was born in Atlanta, Georgia, and she played piano for the church, danced for the church to raise money. She said that they'd pull a curtain down across the pulpit and she'd dance to raise money for the church and she also played for the church. When I was around…

66.t: The first tunes: Fandango and Mother Pin a Rose on Me
66.s: She did not know what she was playing as a baby; later she played a ragtime tune her mother taught her, 'Fandango', and a song her stepfather Fletcher Burley taught her.
66.q: No, when I played the History of Jazz I played the same tune that she taught me... it was a rag-time. we called it 'Fandango' And "Mother Pin a Rose on Me", my stepfather taught me that when I was - I used to play that.

19.t: Born in Red Springs; seeing music through the piano and the hymn book
19.s: Malachi describes the grandmother's pump organ, being quieted as a toddler with a hymn book, and his sense that a gift is really a love for something.
19.q: knowing it, from the time I was born, which is something I am very, very grateful for. People usually say that you're born with a gift or something. Well, I think that if I have a gift, or if anyone has a gift, what it really means is that you have a love for something. And of course, my really...

19.t: Father brings home a five-dollar piano; Uncle Jim's five-dollar offer
19.s: Just before he turns thirteen a used piano arrives, and Uncle Jim promises five dollars to the first child to play something; Malachi learns Lift Every Voice and Sing.
19.q: But the most significant thing about that was that just before my thirteenth birthday... As I said before, my birthday is September 6, and I think it was in August, about the middle of August... That's just before my thirteenth birthday. My uncle and my father came to the house with a truck. It was…

176.t: Billie's musical family, learning piano and first blues
176.s: Billie says her parents and sisters all played piano by ear, mostly in the Baptist church; she learned blues first and later decided with Edna to go into show business.
176.q: All played piano. All my niece's nephew plays piano. Everyone in the family is musical pianos. Yeah. Of course, they take other instruments that they wanted to learn. Some one is trombone, one is sax.

769.t: Family music and his cousin Feast the ragtime pianist
769.s: His first instrument was piano, he played on household objects, and cousin Feast played ragtime and train effects.
769.q: Well, my daddy was, he used to sing in a quartet. Mm-hmm. You know, the old barbershop quartets? Mm-hmm. Back in the early hundreds. 1900s, so he was a bass songster. And he was considered one of the best that they had in the third ward. Yeah, I got it. Well, my first instrument was piano. My…

647.t: Musical family and the family piano
647.s: Mother, siblings and brothers played piano, George trumpet; the family piano he practiced on until he sold it for $25, and his sister the nun.
647.q: My mother played, my older sister played, and my sister, the next to the older sister, played... What instrument? Piano. My oldest brother played piano. My next to the oldest brother played piano. Uh, my brother George, he played trumpet. Oh, somebody wants to see. I'll turn it off for a minute.

263.t: Early music, Baltimore pianists, Peabody, and first pro trio in 1936
263.s: Ewell gives his birth details, early piccolo and piano lessons, his brother's records, Waller and Morton records and collector Bill Riddle, then a short trio tour to Atlantic City and business college.
263.q: We'll start off, I'll always put the data on here such as that we're interviewing Don Ewell and it's at 905 Royal Street and this is Bill Russell and the date is December 1st, 1960. Do you want to give your full name if you have a middle name or anything, Don? Donald Tyson Ewell. And when were you…

194.t: Born in Bogalusa, raised in New Orleans, mother's music
194.s: Born elsewhere, brought to New Orleans at two months, raised near Canal Street; his mother played many instruments and was his first teacher.
194.q: I was born in Bugaloocy, but my mother brought me here when I was about two months old. And I was born around seven or eight blocks, not born, but I was raised about seven or eight blocks from Canal Street, on the south side. On the south side.

195.t: Birth in Palmer, Texas and learning piano from player-piano rolls
195.s: Parker gives his birth details and says his farm parents were not musical. He taught himself at four by copying the notes of player-piano rolls and then phonograph records.
195.q: where you were from, when you were born, and your real name. John Parker, 1918, August the 8th, Palmer, Texas. And were your parents musically inclined? No, we had a cotton farm out there and a player piano that I was interested in all my life and that's about how I got started.

517.t: Mother, sister and starting piano lessons
517.s: His mother, a Gospel minister, played first; his sister, a piano teacher, taught Kenny Barron; Bryant was sent to a teacher.
517.q: Oh she is. She still is. She still teaches piano and she is basically a Gospel pianist, about the best I ever heard. I haven’t heard of anybody better than her. But she’s a teacher and she’s a piano teacher and Kenny Barron was one of her first students. I mean she was Kenny’s first piano teacher.…

440.t: Toronto's pop music, Luigi Romanelli and her older brother
440.s: No real music scene in Toronto; her older brother and his college friends taught her the instruments.
440.q: And then, but I had an older brother that Duke was also very fond of. And he and I would listen and go to things together. And so that way, he and his friends who were going on to

693.t: Mother's 'swing orchestras' quote; first ukulele and no piano at home
693.s: Rowe asks about the quote on the CD title. Grosz recalls his mother, the school ukulele and his father's possible disdain for a bourgeois piano.
693.q: Yes, that was my mother, who was very happy. I had sort of learned secretly, because I don’t know, you know when you really care about something, I really cared. I’m not one of those guys who had an instrument thrust in his hand although I did have a ukulele thrust in my hand when I was about eight…

811.t: Learning dynamics from his father and Oscar Peterson
811.s: Eddie says he learned dynamics early from his songwriter father and admires playing soft with intense beat, as in Oscar Peterson's trio.
811.q: Oh very early. My dad was a piano player in a Dixieland/swing style. He loved ragtime but he couldn’t quite get the stride thing going. So it was just very great. And he wrote songs, he wrote hundreds of songs and arrangements. And so I grew up listening to music, okay, that had dynamics and had…

611.t: Finding the key to his mother's organ
611.s: He tells how he found the hidden key to his religious mother's country organ and she wept when she heard him play; he then had to play hymns often.
611.q: Yeah. I started by ear, see at three years old I just —if I have time I can give you a little short story just how I started playing.

490.t: First piece at four; living behind the church
490.s: He played a church piece at four, and the family lived in flats at the back of the church.
490.q: That happened sometimes, too. Of course I had one like that. I had one girl who’d bring her child to the class. And one day, you know the child would be standing there, and one day I’d just say, “do you what you’re doing here?” She said – she shook her head, said, “yes” and she sat down there and…

225.t: The family upright piano, sisters and church repertoire
225.s: A broken upright at home, a digression on player pianos, and whether his sisters or church pieces figured in his lessons.
225.q: Yes, yes. We had an old upright piano where half the keys did not play. [laughter] It was in dire need of repair, but I did have an instrument on which to practice. I sometimes wonder how we happened to have a piano in the home, but we did.

226.t: The family buys a player piano at Wurlitzer
226.s: His mother could not buy a piano without a man's signature so his uncle signed; it was a piano-roll instrument.
226.q: Yes. At the point – I recall them wanting me to take lessons on the piano – have a piano. Not only that. They socialized. They had friends come over when they had their little soirees and private parties – chitlin’ circuit, as I call it – chitlin’ dinners and all of that kind of stuff. They’d have…

109.t: His mother teaches him piano and dance; her death
109.s: Clarke was born in Pittsburgh; his pianist mother taught him piano from about five, and when she died around age six and a half he gave up music.
109.q: Well, Helen, I was born in Pittsburgh, exactly 63 years ago, and my mother was a very good pianist and she began teaching me to dance and to play the piano. She

1.t: Lu's brother August and the dime for new tunes
1.s: Lu's brother, the fifth August in the family line, paid her a dime for each new tune she hummed.
1.ch: Lu Barker and the Barbarin family
1.q: My father was named August. My brother was named August. He named his son August. And then his son is named August. So now we've got five. We've got August, Senior, August, Junior, August the Third, August the Fourth and August the Fifth.

145.t: Growing up behind the piano; perfect pitch; always a musician
145.s: Royal slept behind the piano as an infant, hummed tunes before talking, has absolute pitch, and never wanted to be anything but a musician.
145.q: That's it. I slept behind the piano from the time I was two or three months old on my father's overcoat. Anytime they would go out of town or across town or anywhere else to keep her in the band, I was the baby back in behind the piano on the overcoats.

9.t: Piano at home and his father's job as head janitor
9.s: A piano was in the parlor but nobody used it; he played by ear, took brief lessons, and describes his father's work at South Station and his mother's day work.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: : Oh, there was always a piano there. My Daddy tried to start the kids off musically, you know. Because at that time, practically all homes had a piano in it.

120.t: Music in the house: his mother and grandmother
120.s: Davison says music was always around him; his mother sang and played piano, and as a baby he pounded pans in time to her playing.
120.q: Well, the first thing that anybody ever says to you when they want to know something about you, they always say - how did you get started? Well, that's a pretty hard thing to describe; I think music doesn't get started; it happens. And, of course, in my house, from the time I was one year old,…

92.t: Mother, grandmother and W. C. Handy in Montgomery
92.s: Collins says his mother and grandmother were fine pianists who taught music, and his mother demonstrated sheet music for W. C. Handy with Fletcher Henderson. They tried to discourage him from playing piano.
92.q: Yes. Well, my mother was a very good pianist, and my grandmother was a very good pianist, and they taught music, played. My mother was something else though. And she also worked at this particular time real early, and when I was very small she worked for W. C. Handy, as a demonstration pianist. She…

93.t: Watching his mother's dancing lessons in Thomasville
93.s: Green says his mother took folk and clog dancing lessons for exercise and brought him along at about three; he watched and fell in love with dancing.
93.q: Well, she used to go to a town called Thomasville, Georgia. That's a little ways from Fitzgerald, Georgia, my birthplace, and she'd taken dancing lessons for just to keep her-- health purposes. You know, that's the she wanted to be trim. It was like an exercise with her, you know. And I was a…

566.t: Selling the family piano and getting rid of her music after her mother died
566.s: She describes singing on the porch as a girl, then how after her mother passed she sold the upright piano for $10 and discarded records, a Basie-gift record player and music. Dance defers the subject.
566.ch: Central High, first records and leaving home
566.q: I used to sit up and play and sing, and people would be walking by and they'd be standing out front and listening, you know. Sometimes they'd come

454.t: Revoicing a childhood tune on piano
454.s: Mingus sings a children's song he always revoiced, putting six chords in it.
454.ch: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
454.q: No, when I (inaudible).^ "Mother, mother, may I go, down to the car and meet my beau?" I always revoiced it, even before I knew what notes were.

124.t: Visiting pianists and the two baby grands
124.s: Pianists from Baltimore and Washington came on weekends to play classical pieces on the two baby grands his father bought for the sun parlor.
124.ch: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
124.q: he would have like -- outstanding piano players would come down from Philly, (inaudible). My mother had a second floor which was really a sun parlor. And in that room my father had bought him two baby grand pianos and it was locked together. And he'd have these different piano players come in…

78.t: Fletcher plays piano at home; parents' classical and church music
78.s: Horace says his brother Fletcher's playing on visits home from Atlanta University inspired him. Their father started their mother and Fletcher on piano young, and the family played only classical and church music.
78.ch: Childhood, first teachers and the Wilberforce Collegians
78.q: Well, naturally, the number one thing -- I was 100 percent influenced, Tom, by my brother, you know, and even before I could play a note, he was playing, and he was going to school at that time in Atlanta University which wasn't too far from home. And he would come home about twice a month, I…

112.t: His mother's organ and the sleeping organ teacher
112.s: His mother plays hymns on the organ; he sneaks ragtime on it while his teacher sleeps.
112.q: My mother had an organ. She used to sing sometimes, "Jesus, lover of all my soul", and I can hear some of these women singing now the way she was just singing. Anyhow, she'd sit down there and play for you with two fingers, "Jesus, lover of all my soul", and belt it out.

79.t: B. Walker, and the player piano at a family friend's home
79.s: A friend, B. Walker, came to the door saying a lady wanted to see Joe. Thomas recalls the family friend who hosted the kids to pump a player piano.
79.ch: Boyhood in Webster Groves and early roadhouse work
79.q: No, it must have been terrible but they did give us that encouragement and there were a lot of little girls there and there was a lot of lemonade and these jack-o-laterns strung places around the palees and listen to me, I've got to tell you this before beea I forget it. I was home during this year…
